cases.name: customer-support
cases.note: The graph as authored: the safe wiring must not be rejected. A validator that rejected everything would score perfectly on the unsafe cases alone.

cases.name: support-platform
cases.note: The composition graph assembles, including the cross-graph capability check (which these graphs satisfy at equality — strictly wider provision is exercised in the validator suite, not here) and the output-side check that each service sub-graph's declared boundary type is the union of the referenced graph's terminal outputs.

cases.name: bypass_pipeline
cases.note: Untrusted input wired straight into the tool-capable node. The blunt mistake: the edge does not type-check.

cases.name: launder_trust
cases.note: The subtle mistake: widen the tool-capable node's input so the edge *does* type-check. Caught instead as upward coercion — trust cannot be laundered by relabelling the consumer.

cases.name: launder_trust_via_variant
cases.note: `launder_trust` disguised by a sum type: one output variant marked untrusted, the other leaving clean. Each variant leaves on its own port, so each must satisfy the lattice on its own.

cases.name: launder_trust_by_declaration
cases.note: `launder_trust` excused by declaring the tool-capable consumer a discharger. The lattice accepts a declared discharger; the sink rule does not let a node holding a tool-scoped client be one.

cases.name: delegate_via_edge
cases.note: A node returns the knowledge-base handle it holds, and a downstream node with no `with` clause for it uses it: reference passing along an edge, the delegation the graph gives up to keep its authority topology static.

cases.name: untrusted_into_tool_node
cases.note: Raw untrusted input into the tool-capable node, labelled consistently so no node raises trust. The lattice alone constrains raising trust, not consuming it; the sink rule keeps untrusted data off a tool-capable node.

cases.name: route_tool_into_inference_slot
cases.note: The platform routes its tool-scoped client into `CustomerSupport`'s inference-only slot. Narrowing is checked, not enforced, so the child's discharger would hold a tool client the sink rule never saw; the cross-graph narrowing check refuses the routing.

cases.name: launder_via_duplicate_role
cases.note: Two variants under one role: the edge check resolved the role to the first, clean variant while the runtime routed both, and raw untrusted input reached the tool-capable node. The type parser rejects a repeated role.

cases.name: hide_branch_behind_whole_edge
cases.note: `NotifyUser` takes `ModerateContent`'s whole labelled sum on an unported edge in place of its violation edge. The runtime routes by role, so the edge never fires and a policy violation is swallowed silently; the validator once read it as covering every variant.

cases.name: hide_branch_behind_unlabelled_variant
cases.note: The same swallowed violation by another spelling: `ModerateContent`'s violation variant loses its role, so no port carries it and variant completeness, which sweeps roles, never saw it. The type parser rejects a partly labelled sum.

cases.name: unreached_audit_node
cases.note: A second node takes the boundary input and no edge reaches it. The runtime chose its entry by file order, so one of the two was skipped silently; a graph runs from exactly one entry node, which every other node is reached from.

cases.name: mislabel_subgraph_output
cases.note: The composition mistake, now caught: a service sub-graph node claims a boundary output (`DeliveryConfirmation`) narrower than the union its terminals actually emit (`DeliveryConfirmation | EscalationTicket`), hiding the escalation path. Every edge still type-checks, so this is invisible to the edge analysis; the output-side cross-graph check catches it — the check that closed the `ServiceOutcome` gap.

cases.name: unevaluatable_contract
cases.note: A different kind of fault from the mutations above: not an unsafe wiring but an unevaluatable specification. A node declares a precondition outside the closed contract vocabulary. It is pinned because the contract layer's value depends on the ceiling being real — a predicate that silently evaluated to false rather than being rejected would make every satisfied contract ambiguous.

the host body mints a handle no clause granted; the component imports an interface it was never granted, so it cannot instantiate — the refusal lands before any guest code runs

escapes.probe: open a socket, holding a clock
escapes.note: one deliberately granted WASI interface (wasi:clocks/wall-clock) does not reopen the ambient world — the grant buys the clock and nothing else

escapes.probe: read a file, holding a clock
escapes.note: the clock grant does not reopen the filesystem either

the host body mints a handle for the host (the PoC performs no network I/O, so this shows minting only); the confined node's refusal is the handle's, identical on either tier for a granted handle — what the confined tier adds is that the body cannot mint another
